expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Presuming Competence with Age-Respectful High-School Access
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A 16-year-old with multiple disabilities and complex communication needs enters high school. Citing her severe intellectual disability label, staff assign preschool nursery-rhyme puzzles in a segregated basement classroom, assume she cannot engage with literature, and skip ecological profiling of her strengths and peer preferences.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Presume competence, complete an ecological profile of strengths, adapt age-respectful high-school literature, and build peer partial participation.
expandableCase.explanation: Best practice for learners with extensive support needs rejects severity-driven expectation ceilings and infantilizing materials. Presuming competence and conducting ecological inventories identify meaningful partial-participation roles and supports that provide authentic access to age-appropriate academic and social environments.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: When interpreting development, context, and variability for a learner with intensive support needs, a kindergarten teacher notices that one child reaches several language milestones later than classmates. What is the most appropriate first interpretation?
choices: Broad developmental patterns allow wide variation, so the team should gather multi-source evidence across settings before drawing conclusions.
Falling below the typical classroom average on language milestones establishes a developmental disability that warrants formal eligibility.
The team should assign a provisional disability label promptly so specialized speech-language interventions can begin before gathering family input.
Chronological age norms become uninformative once a child trails classmates, so expectations should be based on informal adult impressions instead.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Milestones provide useful reference points, not stand-alone diagnoses. Educators should document functioning across domains, contexts, and time and involve qualified team members before attributing a pattern to disability. expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Removing AAC Prerequisites and Modeling Aided Language Input
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A nine-year-old nonspeaking student with Rett syndrome communicates preferences through eye gaze, smiles, and vocalizations. Staff withhold an eye-gaze speech-generating device until she passes a picture-matching prerequisite test, speak on her behalf during routines, and rarely model core symbols on her low-tech gaze board.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Remove prerequisite barriers, launch immediate high- and low-tech AAC access, honor nonsymbolic signals, and train all partners in Aided Language Input.
expandableCase.explanation: Research in augmentative and alternative communication establishes zero cognitive or motor prerequisites for AAC access. Treating nonsymbolic behaviors as communicative while ensuring every adult consistently models core vocabulary through Aided Language Input replaces adult over-speaking and expands autonomous expression.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A learner with severe or profound disabilities uses AAC to select relevant ideas but needs support organizing them in a shared written paragraph. Which response is best?
choices: Have an adult staff member select the ideas and compose each finished paragraph to keep pace with class deadlines.
Model an age-respectful example with AAC access, use a visual organizer, and fade prompts while preserving authorship.
Deliver identical remedial drills across every academic subject regardless of the learner’s demonstrated idea-selection strengths.
Conclude that the learner lacks grade-level ideas to contribute because spoken verbal output is limited during class.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: The instructional response should presume competence, preserve authorship, and target the observed organization need through accessible communication, explicit modeling, guided participation, and systematic prompt fading.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: A learner with severe or profound disabilities shows distress during a noisy group routine but participates in a predictable small group with communication and sensory supports. What perspective is most useful?
choices: Examine interactions among expressive access, environmental load, health, task demands, scaffolds, and outcomes.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Which evidence is essential when planning age-respectful support for a learner with severe or profound disabilities?
choices: One classroom adult’s personal expectations without input from the learner, family, or related-service specialists.
Integrated data on communication, health, sensory-motor access, adaptive-academic skills, preferences, and settings.
A single standardized oral reading score collected during a brief general education screening window.
The student’s primary eligibility label paired with general impressions of physical appearance and diagnosis.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Person-centered planning integrates multiple sources to identify strengths, preferences, access needs, safety considerations, meaningful goals, and supports across environments. Severity labels alone do not determine a program.

chapterTakeaways: Individualize instruction for learners with multiple disabilities, deafblindness, or Cortical Visual Impairment (CVI) using tactile cues, high-contrast reduced-clutter materials, and wait time.
Reject prerequisite myths for AAC: every learner, including pre-symbolic communicators, deserves immediate multimodal access combining touch cues, object calendars, core boards, or SGDs.
Use Aided Language Stimulation (partner-augmented input) by modeling target core symbols on the student's AAC system during natural routines without demanding immediate imitation.

expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Enforcing Feeding Safety, IHP Updates, Positioning, and CVI Access
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A seven-year-old with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy, cortical visual impairment (CVI), seizures, and dysphagia slumps and coughs during lunch. His emergency seizure plan is two years outdated, a substitute aide offers thin liquids contrary to feeding orders, and classroom pages use cluttered black-and-white graphics.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Halt unsafe feeding immediately, update the IHP and seizure protocol with the nurse, schedule PT/OT positioning checks, and apply high-contrast CVI visuals.
expandableCase.explanation: Protecting medically complex learners requires current Individualized Healthcare Plans, strict compliance with dysphagia feeding protocols, and nurse-supervised delegation. Monitoring positioning fatigue reduces aspiration risk, while simplified, high-contrast visual layouts remove sensory access barriers linked to CVI.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: When removing sensory, physical, communication, or health access barriers, a student with low vision receives a worksheet containing a dense unlabeled diagram. What is the best access response?
choices: Provide a classmate’s completed responses so the student can record the conclusions without interpreting the figure.
Allow extended time on the original worksheet while keeping the dense visual graphic unchanged in size and contrast.
Provide an equivalent accessible format—such as a verbal description, tactile graphic, or usable enlargement.
Substitute an easier vocabulary activity from an earlier unit so the student can work independently without visual media.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Access means preserving the intended concept while changing how information is perceived when necessary. The appropriate representation depends on the learner’s assessed media and access needs. knowledgeChecks.prompt: When removing sensory, physical, communication, or health access barriers, a student who is deaf uses sign language and will join a fast-paced seminar. Which plan best supports communication access?
choices: Replace live seminar discussions with written summaries so the student can earn participation credit independently.
Maintain rapid open-floor discussions without turn-taking cues so the student experiences realistic peer pacing.
Assign front-row seating near the teacher’s desk as the primary accommodation for full seminar participation.
Address expressive modality, direct interaction, acoustics, assistive technology, and clear speaker visibility.

Third, the team performs an environmental demand analysis across general-education, school, and community routines to pinpoint physical, sensory, or communication barriers rather than defaulting to segregation. Fourth, teams design least intrusive supports and partial-participation adaptations using chronological-age-appropriate materials—strictly avoiding infantilization of older learners. Finally, teachers embed systematic instruction inside natural routines with peer-mediated social inclusion, continuously expanding student autonomy as competence grows.

Ecological Profile & Family Context: Conduct a strengths and interests inventory alongside a cultural family context review to center meaningful learner preferences.
Environmental Demand Analysis: Map real-world steps, sensory loads, and participation barriers in natural school and community settings to eliminate unnecessary segregation.

diagrams.title: Multimodal Communication, Switch Access & AAC Implementation Cycle
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Build an accessible, presume-competence AAC system by mapping presymbolic and symbolic communication, evaluating motor and sensory access methods, delivering partner-assisted core vocabulary modeling, and generalizing communication across daily routines.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow moving from communication-matrix mapping and motor/sensory access evaluation to partner-assisted AAC modeling, core vocabulary expansion, and cross-routine generalization.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right AAC cycle from presymbolic/symbolic communication mapping through motor/sensory access assessment, aided language modeling with core vocabulary, and communicative function expansion to generalization across routines.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, the team—with family and speech-language pathologist (SLP) leadership—maps all current presymbolic and symbolic communication forms (vocalizations, facial expressions, gestures, object cues, pictures, signs, or speech-generating devices) without requiring cognitive prerequisites for AAC. Second, OT, PT, SLP, and vision/hearing specialists evaluate reliable motor, visual, and auditory access methods including direct selection, eye gaze, tactile symbols, or single/dual switch scanning. Third, communication partners deliver aided language input—modeling high-frequency core vocabulary (e.g., more, stop, go, help, like, different) plus personalized fringe words on the learner’s system during natural exchanges. Fourth, teams expand communicative functions beyond requesting to include protesting, commenting, greeting, asking questions, and directing care. Finally, AAC systems remain available across classrooms, home, and community settings so communication generalizes to peers and unfamiliar partners, feeding vocabulary and access updates back to the communication profile.

Partner-Assisted Modeling & Core Vocabulary: Provide frequent aided language input by pointing to or activating robust core vocabulary plus personalized fringe words on the student’s AAC system without demanding hand-over-hand compliance.

Expand Communicative Functions: Move beyond requesting snacks or toys to honor refusal/protesting, commenting, asking questions, sharing feelings, social closeness, and self-advocacy across instructional tasks.

Cross-Routine & Partner Generalization: Ensure low-tech and high-tech AAC backups travel across every school, home, and community routine with peers and family, updating vocabulary and access settings as skills grow.

diagrams.title: Comprehensive Health, Positioning, Sensory & Collaborative Care Coordination Flow

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right care coordination flow from IHP and emergency protocols through PT/OT/nursing positioning and sensory access, paraprofessional delegation boundaries, and privacy-respecting care to active engagement.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, the school nurse, family, and medical providers establish an Individualized Healthcare Plan (IHP) and emergency action plans covering seizure response, safe feeding/dysphagia precautions, suctioning, and respiratory monitoring. Second, physical therapists, occupational therapists, vision/hearing specialists, and nurses align therapeutic positioning schedules, adaptive seating, safe lifting transfers, and sensory access adjustments (lighting, contrast, acoustic clarity, tactile cues). Third, the special educator and licensed nurse maintain strict scope-of-practice and paraprofessional delegation boundaries—providing documented competency training while never delegating licensed nursing judgment or instructional design. Fourth, personal care and health routines are scheduled discreetly to protect student privacy, autonomy, and bodily dignity. Finally, integrated health and positioning supports maximize alertness, comfort, and active instructional participation, with any change in fatigue, skin integrity, or medical status looping immediately back to IHP review.

diagrams.title: Lifespan Transition, Self-Determination, Choice-Making & Supported Community Living Flow

Second, educators embed daily choice-making, preference expression, self-advocacy, and least-restrictive supported decision-making agreements rather than defaulting automatically to full guardianship. Fourth, with informed family consent, schools initiate early interagency linkages to vocational rehabilitation, developmental disability waivers, Medicaid/SSI benefits planning, and pediatric-to-adult medical care coordination before entitlement under IDEA ends. diagrams.title: Systematic Instruction: Errorless Learning, Time Delay & Chaining Sequence
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Design and execute systematic, errorless instruction for students with severe and profound disabilities using ecological task analysis, time-delay and prompt-fading procedures, immediate reinforcement, and planned generalization.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow detailing systematic instruction from ecological task analysis through time delay, chaining, and prompt fading to reinforcement thinning and generalization.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right systematic instruction flow from ecological task analysis through time delay and chaining, immediate specific reinforcement, and data-driven prompt fading to setting and partner generalization.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, the educator conducts an ecological task analysis—breaking an academic or functional routine into observable, age-appropriate steps with natural discriminative cues and individualized partial-participation adaptations. Second, the teacher selects a matching response-prompting and chaining strategy: constant or progressive time delay (starting at 0-second delay for errorless acquisition before shifting to 3–5 seconds), system of least prompts, or most-to-least fading paired with forward, backward, or total-task chaining. Third, correct unprompted and prompted responses earn immediate, behavior-specific reinforcement paired with natural consequences and gentle error correction that avoids practicing mistakes. Fourth, trial-by-trial data drive systematic prompt fading and reinforcement thinning so the learner transfers stimulus control from adult prompts to natural environmental cues without prompt dependence. Finally, skills are actively generalized across novel materials, settings, and communication partners, looping back to task-analysis adaptations whenever step-level barriers appear.
textEquivalent: Ecological Task Analysis & Natural Cues: Break functional or academic routines into observable steps anchored to natural environmental cues, incorporating individualized partial-participation adaptations where needed.

Errorless Time Delay, Chaining & Prompt Selection: Pair constant or progressive time delay (0-second errorless trials shifting to wait intervals) or most-to-least fading with forward, backward, or total-task chaining matched to the skill.

Immediate Specific Reinforcement & Error Correction: Deliver prompt, preference-assessed reinforcement for independent and prompted responses, using brief non-punitive error interruption so errors are not rehearsed.

Data-Driven Prompt Fading & Schedule Thinning: Review trial-by-trial independence data to systematically fade intrusive prompts and thin artificial reinforcers to natural schedules, preventing prompt dependence.

Generalization Across Settings, Materials & Partners: Program generalization explicitly across multiple exemplars, classrooms, community settings, and staff or peers, revising task steps if performance stalls.

diagrams.title: Accessible Assessment Selection, Construct-vs-Access Alignment & Administration Flow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Select and administer valid, accessible assessments for learners with severe and profound disabilities by separating target constructs from motor or sensory access barriers, aligning AAC/AT and linguistic supports, pacing administration with familiar partners, and documenting authentic portfolio performance.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right accessible assessment flow from construct-vs-access differentiation through AAC/AT and linguistic validity alignment, fatigue-paced adapted administration, and ecological portfolio rubrics to valid instructional interpretation.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, the team separates the target cognitive or academic construct from motor, visual, hearing, or speech access barriers so motor or communication limits are never confounded with intellectual ability. Second, evaluators select universally accessible tools aligned to alternate achievement standards or formative probes, ensuring full AAC, assistive technology, and home-language validity rather than English-only or inaccessible norm-referenced tests. Third, familiar trained partners administer assessments using the student’s everyday adapted response modes (eye gaze, switch scanning, partner-assisted scanning, or tactile selection) on fatigue-paced schedules without arbitrary timed-test barriers. Fourth, teams document authentic routine performance through observational rubrics and structured ecological portfolios across settings. Finally, educators interpret evidence cautiously to guide immediate instructional adjustments and verify whether any access barrier still suppressed demonstrated competence.

Third, evaluators triangulate adaptive behavior across home, school, and community environments alongside dynamic assessment of learning potential (teach-test-retest with scaffolds) to avoid single-setting bias. Fourth, the team practices cautious score interpretation—synthesizing multiple-disability profiles without overrelying on floor-effect IQ cutoffs or allowing diagnostic overshadowing to mask sensory or communication needs. Finally, the team translates eligibility findings into concrete instructional, communication, health, and access supports for the IEP, scheduling triennial or earlier re-evaluations whenever student needs change.

accessibility.longDescription: Read from top to bottom. First, IEP teams anchor decisions in IDEA FAPE, Least Restrictive Environment (LRE), and the least dangerous assumption—never assigning automatic separate-school or segregated placements based on disability label or support intensity. Second, districts uphold procedural safeguards by delivering Prior Written Notice (PWN) in accessible native language, obtaining informed parental consent before evaluation or initial services, and guaranteeing transparent IEP record access. Third, teams document individualized LRE placement justifications after considering supplementary aids and services, and apply rigorous state eligibility criteria before recommending an alternate assessment on alternate academic achievement standards. Fourth, educators enforce Manifestation Determination Review (MDR) protections to prevent unlawful disciplinary exclusion or informal send-homes when communication or sensory distress drives behavior. Finally, staff safeguard sensitive medical and IEP records under FERPA and prepare families early for age-of-majority rights transfer and supported decision-making options.
textEquivalent: FAPE, LRE & Least Dangerous Assumption: Guarantee meaningful educational benefit in the Least Restrictive Environment, rejecting automatic separate-school placement driven by disability category.

Equitable LRE & Alternate-Assessment Criteria: Justify any removal from general education only after supplementary aids are considered, and apply formal eligibility criteria for alternate assessments.
MDR Protections Against Unlawful Exclusion: Convene Manifestation Determination Reviews for removals exceeding 10 days and prohibit informal send-homes or exclusionary discipline tied to disability.

Third, teachers engage in post-unit outcome reflection and targeted professional development—continuously upskilling in AAC, assistive technology, and evidence-based systematic instruction while rejecting unvalidated interventions. Fourth, educators strengthen schoolwide capacity through peer mentoring, coaching, and sustainable team boundaries that prevent caregiver and educator burnout. Finally, professionals champion inclusive school-culture leadership and student self-advocacy systems, refusing to accept unnecessary exclusion and feeding student dignity outcomes back into ongoing ethical reflection.

Build an accessible, presume-competence AAC system by mapping presymbolic and symbolic communication, evaluating motor and sensory access methods, delivering partner-assisted core vocabulary modeling, and generalizing communication across daily routines.

Coordinate Individualized Healthcare Plans (IHPs), medical emergency protocols, therapeutic positioning and sensory access, legal paraprofessional delegation boundaries, and dignified active learning engagement.

Build dignity-centered lifespan transition plans uniting person-centered futures planning with student and family, daily choice-making and supported decision-making, community-based living and customized employment, and seamless adult-agency and medical transition linkages.

Design and execute systematic, errorless instruction for students with severe and profound disabilities using ecological task analysis, time-delay and prompt-fading procedures, immediate reinforcement, and planned generalization.

Connect grade-level core academic standards to alternate achievement access points, embedded IEP communication and motor goals, natural peer supports, and genuine general-education belonging in the Least Restrictive Environment (LRE).

Select and administer valid, accessible assessments for learners with severe and profound disabilities by separating target constructs from motor or sensory access barriers, aligning AAC/AT and linguistic supports, pacing administration with familiar partners, and documenting authentic portfolio performance.

Execute timely, nondiscriminatory multidisciplinary evaluations for students with severe, profound, or multiple disabilities by honoring IDEA timelines without RTI delay, triangulating family history and adaptive behavior across settings, applying dynamic assessment, and translating findings into instructional needs.

Establish valid, accessible progress monitoring and alternate assessment evidence by defining functional and academic IEP targets via ecological inventories, collecting systematic trial-by-trial and portfolio data, verifying inter-observer fidelity and access supports, and adjusting instruction.

Safeguard the legal and ethical rights of students with severe and profound disabilities by applying the least dangerous assumption, delivering accessible native-language PWN and informed consent, justifying LRE and alternate-assessment decisions equitably, enforcing MDR protections, and upholding FERPA health privacy and age-of-majority transition.

Coordinate families, related-service providers, general educators, and paraprofessionals through a transdisciplinary model using shared IEP matrices, push-in therapy integration, coached paraprofessional prompting without proximity isolation, and natural peer-support facilitation.

Maintain ethical, safe, and evidence-based practice for students with severe and profound disabilities by verifying nursing and therapy scope-of-practice limits, fulfilling mandated-reporting duties, engaging in ongoing AAC/AT and EBP professional learning, coaching colleagues, and building dignity and inclusion advocacy systems.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: Ecological profiling & presumed competence in inclusive classrooms
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Replace Mental-Age Exclusion with Presumed Competence and Grade 7 Partial Participation
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Challenge a deficit-based placement recommendation for a seventh-grade student with complex motor and communication needs by constructing an ecological inventory, age-respectful Grade 7 access plan, and peer-supported participation matrix.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Maya (Grade 7, Rett syndrome with hand apraxia and nonspeaking profile) uses eye gaze to choose music, greet classmates, and laugh at teen comics. A draft report labels her "functioning at an 18-month level" and proposes moving her out of Grade 7 science and ELA into a separate room to sort plastic preschool bears. Her parents emphasize that Maya stays alert during peer labs and responds strongly to age-appropriate novels read aloud.
taskParts: Critique the "18-month mental age" label and preschool-bear task using presumed competence, age-appropriateness, and IDEA Least Restrictive Environment (LRE) principles.
Conduct an ecological inventory and discrepancy analysis for Grade 7 science and ELA to design meaningful partial participation and adapted grade-aligned academic access.
Specify natural peer supports and an embedded instruction matrix so Maya practices her IEP communication and literacy goals alongside seventh-grade classmates.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Center Maya's purposeful eye-gaze selections, engagement with teen comics and read-aloud novels, and alertness in peer labs rather than a flawed developmental-age equivalent that confounds hand apraxia with intellect.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply IDEA Part B LRE and general-curriculum access mandates (34 CFR 300.114 and 300.320), CEC initial special-education standards on dignity and high expectations, and the principle of partial participation.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Embed eye-gaze partner choices, adapted Grade 7 text summaries with core vocabulary overlays, switch-activated lab timers/recordings, and structured peer-support roles inside general-education routines.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Collect embedded trial data on Maya's eye-gaze comprehension responses and peer communicative turns during Grade 7 lessons, reviewing inclusion fidelity and adult-proximity fading monthly.

successCriteria: Explicitly rejects mental-age labeling and preschool sorting materials as violations of chronological age-appropriateness and presumed competence.
Uses ecological inventory and discrepancy analysis to adapt Grade 7 science and ELA routines rather than removing Maya to a segregated classroom.
Designs concrete partial-participation adaptations (eye-gaze response boards, adapted Grade 7 text, switch-activated lab contributions) aligned to standards.
Builds natural peer supports and schedules fading of hovering paraprofessional proximity so classmates interact directly with Maya.
commonPitfalls: Accepting the 18-month age-equivalent score as justification for toddler toys and segregated life-skills drills.
Confusing hand apraxia and absence of speech with inability to understand seventh-grade literature or science concepts.
Placing Maya in Grade 7 science as a passive observer parked at the back of the room without an active communication or response role.
Assigning a one-to-one adult to whisper answers or hover continuously, blocking authentic peer relationships.
sampleOutline: Presumed competence critique: Age-equivalent scores confound Maya's severe hand apraxia with cognition; substituting preschool bear sorting violates age-respectful practice and IDEA LRE access to Grade 7 curriculum.
Ecological inventory: Map typical Grade 7 ELA and science routines (shared reading, lab data recording, group wrap-up) and identify exact motor/communication barriers to solve via adaptation.

Grade-aligned partial participation: Provide adapted Grade 7 novel excerpts with eye-gaze comprehension choices, a switch-activated voice output device to announce lab steps, and peer-partnered lab tables.
Embedded measurement: Track Maya's independent eye-gaze literacy/science responses and peer-directed communicative turns across three weekly lessons while monitoring adult-prompt fading.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: IHP health safety, positioning & paraprofessional delegation
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Enforce IHP Feeding, Positioning, and Nursing Delegation Boundaries Safely
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Resolve urgent health, positioning, and staffing-boundary gaps for a third-grade student with complex medical and motor support needs by coordinating the Individualized Healthcare Plan (IHP), therapy protocols, and legal delegation rules.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Ethan (Grade 3, spastic quadriplegia, G-tube, honey-thickened liquids, focal seizures) needs 90-degree pelvic-trunk alignment at meals and a written seizure protocol. Yesterday a new paraprofessional gave him unthickened juice after he coughed, tried a solo two-person lift without his gait belt, and asked the special educator to train her on G-tube bolus feeds since the school nurse comes only twice weekly.
taskParts: Identify the immediate aspiration, musculoskeletal transfer, and medical-delegation hazards in Ethan's current school routine and state the required emergency response.

Clarify the distinct legal and professional scope-of-practice roles of the school nurse (RN), PT/OT, special educator, and paraprofessional regarding the IHP, G-tube feeds, thickened-liquid dysphagia protocols, and two-person transfers.
Design a documented training, sign-off, positioning-schedule, and emergency-action verification plan integrated with Ethan's IEP health services under IDEA Part B.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Flag the three acute safety breaches: giving unthickened juice after coughing (aspiration risk), executing an unauthorized solo transfer without a gait belt, and requesting non-nurse training on G-tube bolus feeds.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply IDEA Part B school health services mandates (related services for medical access), CEC safety and supervision ethics, and state Nurse Practice Act delegation rules reserving clinical training and G-tube delegation to a licensed RN.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Halt unauthorized practices immediately, convene the RN, PT, OT, SLP, family, and administrator to update the IHP and Emergency Action Plan, post visual positioning/dysphagia guides, and schedule RN-led competency sign-offs.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Require documented RN competency verification before any delegated health procedure, enforce strict two-person transfer staffing logs, track repositioning intervals for skin integrity, and maintain confidential quick-access seizure plans.

successCriteria: Explicitly prohibits the special educator from training or delegating G-tube feeds, identifying clinical medical delegation and competency sign-off as a licensed school nurse (RN) responsibility.
Recognizes unthickened juice paired with coughing as an urgent aspiration hazard requiring strict adherence to SLP/physician dysphagia orders and immediate RN/family notification.
Addresses PT/OT-guided 90-degree pelvic alignment, safe two-person transfer mechanics, and pressure-relief repositioning schedules.
Integrates the IHP and Seizure Action Plan into Ethan's IEP related health services while respecting FERPA confidentiality and staff emergency readiness.
commonPitfalls: Having the special educator demonstrate G-tube feeding to the paraprofessional to cover days when the school nurse is off campus.
Offering small sips of regular water or juice to "clear a cough," which sharply increases silent or overt aspiration risk.
Allowing one adult to complete a transfer when a colleague is running late rather than enforcing mandatory two-person or mechanical-lift protocols.
Keeping Ethan's seizure and aspiration protocols locked solely in the main-office binder instead of accessible confidentially to all trained staff accompanying him.
sampleOutline: Immediate hazard containment: Stop all unauthorized oral thin liquids, solo lifts, and non-RN G-tube instruction immediately; notify the school nurse, administrator, and Ethan's family regarding the aspiration incident.

Scope-of-practice boundaries: The RN authors the IHP, coordinates physician orders, and conducts any legally permitted medical delegation/supervision; the SLP/OT/PT set dysphagia and positioning protocols; the special educator supervises instructional routines.

Coordinated safety protocols: Embed jargon-free visual mealtime alignment checklists (90-degree pelvis/trunk, pacing, honey-thick verification), scheduled two-person lift coverage, and seizure-response drills for every assigned adult.
Accountability and dignity: Document RN and PT/OT competency sign-offs, verify daily positioning and feeding logs, and maintain Ethan's full inclusive participation safely alongside peers.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: Multimodal AAC, switch-access feature matching & partner scanning
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Match Multimodal AAC and Partner-Assisted Scanning for Complex Visual-Motor Needs
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Design a feature-matched, multimodal Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) access plan and partner-modeling routine for a fifth-grade student with cortical visual impairment and severe motor apraxia.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Zara (Grade 5, cortical visual impairment [CVI Phase II], dystonic quadriplegia, and complex communication needs) reliably activates a right-cheek head switch and turns toward high-contrast yellow targets on black backgrounds when visual clutter is minimal. An outside consultant left a 60-cell glossy tablet grid that Zara ignores, leading staff to claim she "is not ready for AAC" and must first master cause-and-effect toys for a year.
taskParts: Refute the "not ready for AAC" prerequisite claim and analyze why the cluttered 60-cell glossy tablet grid failed to match Zara's CVI and motor-access profile.

Conduct a multidisciplinary feature-matching plan (SLP, OT, TVI, special educator, family) pairing her reliable head-switch access with auditory-visual scanning, high-contrast reduced-array symbols, and low-tech partner-assisted scanning.
Establish an Aided Language Stimulation (partner modeling) and daily communication-opportunity routine across academic, social, and transition periods without waiting for prerequisite mastery.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Connect Zara's reliable right-cheek switch activation and visual response to high-contrast yellow-on-black low-clutter targets against the mismatched 60-cell glossy tablet grid.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply IDEA Part B assistive technology and communication special-factor requirements, zero-prerequisite AAC evidence, and multidisciplinary feature matching across sensory (CVI), motor, and linguistic domains.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Deploy a low-glare, high-contrast core-vocabulary array with auditory-visual switch scanning plus a portable partner-assisted scanning flipbook, and train every partner in Aided Language Stimulation with extended wait time.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Collect daily data across communicative functions (requesting, protesting, commenting, answering academic questions), audit battery/switch mounting reliability daily, and ensure AAC travels seamlessly between home and school.

successCriteria: Explicitly rejects cognitive or cause-and-effect prerequisites for AAC access, diagnosing the failure as an environmental and feature-matching mismatch rather than a student deficit.
Integrates CVI accommodations (matte anti-glare surfaces, high-contrast color-on-black targets, reduced visual complexity, controlled lighting) with Zara's reliable right-cheek switch movement.
Builds a true multimodal system combining high-tech auditory-visual switch scanning with low-tech partner-assisted scanning and natural gestures/vocalizations so Zara is never without a voice.
Embeds Aided Language Stimulation (modeling core words without demanding immediate imitation) and generous expectant pause time across all Grade 5 settings.
commonPitfalls: Removing robust AAC to drill isolated cause-and-effect switch toys for a year before allowing communicative vocabulary.
Forcing direct finger pointing or keeping a dense 60-cell glossy grid despite CVI Phase II visual complexity and dystonic motor barriers.
Treating AAC strictly as a device for requesting snacks while omitting protesting, social joking, and Grade 5 academic commenting.
Testing Zara with constant "show me X" commands instead of modeling core vocabulary naturally through Aided Language Stimulation.
sampleOutline: Reframing readiness: There are no prerequisites for AAC; Zara ignored the 60-cell glossy grid because glare, visual clutter, and direct-touch demands mismatched her CVI Phase II and motor profile.

Multidisciplinary feature matching: Partner with the SLP, OT, and Teacher of Students with Visual Impairments (TVI) to configure a matte, high-contrast black-background core array accessed via her right-cheek head switch with auditory preview scanning.

Multimodal redundancy: Pair the speech-generating system with a low-tech high-contrast partner-assisted scanning book and honor Zara's eye gaze, facial expressions, and vocalizations during bathing, recess, or device charging.

Partner instruction and tracking: Train classroom adults and peers in Aided Language Stimulation and 10-to-15-second wait time, tracking independent communicative turns across diverse functions weekly.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: Systematic instruction, constant time delay & chaining
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Eliminate Prompt Dependence Through Task Analysis, Chaining, and Constant Time Delay
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Redesign an inconsistent vocational-and-daily-living instructional routine for a ninth-grade student with severe intellectual disability and autism using systematic task analysis, chaining, constant time delay, and planned generalization.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Owen (Grade 9, severe intellectual disability and autism) restocks school-cafe napkin dispensers using a 10-step picture checklist. Over six weeks he completes only 2 of 10 steps independently because staff give rapid verbal cues and immediate hand-over-hand help after any one-second pause. He waits motionless for adult touch before step 3, and his routine does not transfer to the library supply cart.
taskParts: Diagnose how staff's one-second verbal and hand-over-hand interventions created prompt dependence, and explain why systematic errorless prompting outperforms unsystematic trial-and-error corrections.

Design a 10-step task analysis paired with an explicit chaining procedure (total-task, forward, or backward) and a Constant Time Delay (CTD) schedule transitioning from 0-second to 4-second delay intervals.
Build a systematic generalization and prompt-fading data sheet so Owen transfers independent work routines from the school cafe to the library cart and community settings.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Link Owen's 2-of-10 independent step ceiling, motionless waiting at step 3, and lack of transfer to the library cart directly to staff jumping in after one second with verbal and hand-over-hand prompts.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply evidence-based systematic instruction for learners with extensive support needs: task analysis, chaining, constant time delay (0-second errorless to fixed delay), most-to-least fading, and multiple-exemplar generalization.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Pair a visual step checklist with total-task chaining and Constant Time Delay (0-second controlling prompt during acquisition, then fixed 4-second wait before a gestural/model prompt), reinforcing unprompted steps differentially.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Score each task-analysis step daily by prompt level (independent, gestural, model, partial physical), set objective fade criteria, check interobserver staff fidelity, and probe generalization in the library weekly.

successCriteria: Accurately diagnoses adult-induced prompt dependence caused by one-second verbal chatter and immediate hand-over-hand intervention.
Correctly structures Constant Time Delay (0-second delay trials first for errorless acquisition, then shifting systematically to a consistent 4-second wait interval to invite independent initiation).
Selects and justifies a chaining method (such as total-task chaining with a picture checklist) and differential reinforcement favoring independent responses over prompted ones.
Embeds explicit generalization strategies (multiple settings, varied materials, natural cues, and fading adult proximity) alongside step-by-step prompt-level data collection.
commonPitfalls: Continuing hand-over-hand assistance while verbally repeating directions, which deepens prompt dependence and compromises student bodily autonomy.
Jumping straight to a long wait interval without initial 0-second errorless trials when Owen has not yet learned a new step, leading to repeated errors and frustration.
Recording only a global "completed job with help" checkmark instead of step-by-step independence and prompt-level data.
Assuming mastery in the school cafe will automatically generalize to the library supply cart without training across multiple exemplars and natural cues.
sampleOutline: Prompt-dependence analysis: Immediate 1-second verbal and hand-over-hand interventions turned adult touch into the discriminative stimulus for step 3, blocking independent initiation.

Task analysis and CTD protocol: Break cafe restocking into 10 observable steps paired with a visual strip; run 0-second controlling-prompt trials on unlearned steps, then move to a strict 4-second Constant Time Delay before delivering the least-intrusive effective prompt.

Differential reinforcement and autonomy: Deliver richer praise and preferred reinforcers for unprompted steps than prompted steps, replacing intrusive hand-over-hand guidance with visual/model cues and natural task endpoints.

Generalization and data tracking: Graph percent of independent steps daily across staff, run fidelity checks on the 4-second pause rule, and train across both cafe and library supply carts using natural environmental cues.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: AA-AAS construct-vs-access assessment & FCT behavior support
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Ensure Construct-Valid AA-AAS Assessment and Function-Based Communication Support
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Address both an inaccessible state alternate-assessment plan and escalating self-injurious behavior for an eighth-grade student with deaf-blindness and multiple disabilities by aligning construct-valid AA-AAS access with medical rule-out and Functional Communication Training (FCT).
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Nadia (Grade 8, deaf-blindness with residual low vision, tactile sign, and object-calendar routines) qualifies for the state AA-AAS. Her team plans to give standard paper-print AA-AAS items without tactile graphics or an intervener. Over three weeks, Nadia began biting her wrist during abrupt transitions and unannounced table tasks, and her mother reported mild ear-pulling at home.
taskParts: Evaluate the AA-AAS administration plan using construct-versus-access validity principles, explaining how omitting tactile/intervener accommodations invalidates academic measurement and violates IDEA assessment participation rules.
Outline the required medical/pain rule-out and accessible Functional Behavior Assessment (FBA) steps before finalizing a behavioral hypothesis for Nadia's wrist-biting.

Design a proactive Functional Communication Training (FCT) and antecedent transition plan (tactile object calendars, touch cues, finish-or-break tactile sign) that protects Nadia's safety without aversive or restrictive practices.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Connect Nadia's deaf-blind sensory profile (tactile sign, residual low vision, object calendar), paper-only AA-AAS barrier, abrupt-transition wrist-biting, and home ear-pulling indicating possible acute pain or ear infection.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply IDEA Part B assessment participation and AA-AAS guidelines (34 CFR 300.160), construct-versus-access validity, mandatory medical/sensory rule-out prior to FBA conclusions, and evidence-based FCT.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Secure tactile/braille/large-print AA-AAS formats with trained intervener access aligned to daily instruction, refer for immediate medical/otologic screening, and teach an instant tactile-sign/object cue for "wait," "break," or "hurts."

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Track daily transition predictability, independent FCT tactile-sign requests, and wrist-biting frequency/intensity; prohibit aversive consequences; and verify family consent and nurse/physician follow-up.

successCriteria: Distinguishes the measured academic construct from sensory access barriers, insisting that AA-AAS administration mirror Nadia's daily tactile, low-vision, and intervener accommodations.
Prioritizes immediate medical and dental/otologic rule-out (given recent onset of wrist-biting plus ear-pulling) before attributing self-injury solely to learned behavior.
Designs a function-matched FCT plan teaching an accessible, rapid tactile-sign or tangible-symbol replacement response alongside predictable touch cues and object-calendar transition warnings.
Rejects physical restraint or punitive loss of preferred sensory items, grounding safety responses in proactive de-escalation and continuous team-family data review.
commonPitfalls: Administering visual paper-print AA-AAS items and concluding Nadia lacks Grade 8 alternate academic comprehension when the score only reflects inaccessible print.
Launching behavioral extinction (ignoring wrist-biting) before ruling out ear pain, sinus infection, or sensory shock from unannounced touch.
Assuming AA-AAS eligibility automatically excuses Nadia from grade-aligned standards or removes her right to testing accommodations.
Expecting Nadia to use an unfamiliar multi-step AAC sequence during distress instead of a rapid, low-effort tactile sign or object symbol that immediately honors her request.
sampleOutline: Construct-valid AA-AAS access: Under IDEA Part B, AA-AAS must measure alternate Grade 8 academic content rather than vision/hearing barriers; embed tactile graphics, enlarged high-contrast materials, and a trained intervener matching daily instruction.

Medical rule-out first: Because wrist-biting emerged over three weeks alongside home ear-pulling, immediately coordinate with Nadia's parents and school nurse for medical/otologic evaluation to rule out pain.

Antecedent predictability and FCT: Introduce consistent touch cues and a tactile object calendar two minutes before every transition, and teach a low-effort tactile sign or textured card for "stop/break" reinforced immediately.
Ethical safety monitoring: Log transition antecedents, FCT usage, and self-injury duration daily, avoiding aversive punishments and reviewing progress jointly with the family, TVI/TODHH, and SLP.
