constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Coordinate Transdisciplinary Role Release and Adult Interagency Handoff Before Age-21 Exit
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Design a person-centered, transdisciplinary transition and interagency coordination plan for a 19-year-old student with profound multiple disabilities approaching IDEA exit so his communication, health, community inclusion, and adult services transfer without gaps.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Isaiah (age 19, profound multiple disabilities, head-array power chair, eye-gaze AAC, suctioning needs) attends a district 18-21 program. His PT, OT, SLP, nurse, and teacher run isolated pull-out sessions with conflicting seating and AAC routines. No adult DD waiver, Medicaid, or VR representative has been invited to his IEP, and staff told his mother to seek plenary guardianship immediately.
taskParts: Contrast Isaiah's current fragmented multidisciplinary pull-out model with a true transdisciplinary teaming model featuring structured role release, integrated therapy inside community routines, and unified seating/AAC/health protocols.

Design a person-centered transition and interagency handoff timeline (with parental/student consent to invite adult DD, Medicaid waiver, and vocational agencies) alongside an actionable Summary of Performance (SOP).

Evaluate the staff's plenary-guardianship directive by explaining transfer of rights at age of majority, less-restrictive supported decision-making alternatives, and ethical boundaries against educators giving legal advice.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Address Isaiah's age (19, approaching 21/22 exit), head-array power mobility, eye-gaze AAC, suctioning care, conflicting pull-out therapy routines, absent adult agency invitations, and improper guardianship directive.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply IDEA Part B transition interagency invitation rules (requiring prior consent), Summary of Performance requirements, transfer-of-rights notice rules, transdisciplinary teaming principles, and CEC family-empowerment ethics.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Facilitate a person-centered MAPS/PATH meeting centering Isaiah's eye-gaze preferences, unify PT/OT/SLP/RN protocols into community volunteer/recreation settings, and execute consent-backed invitations to adult DD/Medicaid/VR liaisons.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Maintain a 24-month exit countdown checklist tracking adult waiver waitlists, portable AAC/wheelchair funding ownership, updated health care plans, and objective community-participation outcomes.

successCriteria: Replaces fragmented pull-out therapy with transdisciplinary role release (cross-discipline coaching with clear RN safety limits on suctioning) embedded in real adult community settings.

Corrects the improper plenary-guardianship directive by presenting less-restrictive options (supported decision-making, power of attorney, representative payee) and referring the family to qualified legal/advocacy resources.
Specifies obtaining prior written consent before inviting outside adult agencies (DD services, Medicaid waiver, vocational rehabilitation) to Isaiah's transition IEP.
Details a comprehensive Summary of Performance (SOP) plus equipment/AAC ownership and health-plan continuity steps to prevent the post-school "services cliff."
commonPitfalls: Telling Isaiah's mother that plenary guardianship is legally mandatory for every young adult with severe disabilities, stripping self-determination rights without exploring supported decision-making.
Inviting adult DD or vocational rehabilitation representatives to the IEP meeting without first securing written consent from the adult student or authorized parent.
Allowing PT, OT, and SLP to run separate therapy goals in clinic rooms rather than aligning positioning, eye-gaze communication, and head-array mobility during authentic community activities.
Waiting until the final month before age-21 exit to discover that Isaiah's school-owned eye-gaze AAC device will not follow him into adult life.
sampleOutline: Transdisciplinary integration: Shift PT, OT, SLP, and transition staff to shared community routines with unified seating, eye-gaze AAC overlays, and RN-supervised suctioning protocols via disciplined role release.

Person-centered planning and self-determination: Host a MAPS/PATH session incorporating Isaiah's eye-gaze choices; replace the blanket plenary-guardianship push with unbiased information on supported decision-making and independent legal-aid referrals.

Consent-based interagency handoff: Obtain prior written consent to invite adult DD waiver, Medicaid home-health, and vocational rehabilitation liaisons now so funding, nursing coverage, and personal AAC device funding finalize before exit.

Exit continuity package: Deliver an individualized Summary of Performance documenting Isaiah's eye-gaze communication profile, seating/transfer guides, health protocols, and preferred adult community environments.
constructedResponseWorkshops.reviewNote: Independent applied case-analysis practice; not an official ETS prompt, rubric, score, pass prediction, or eligibility/licensure determination. AlloFlow does not score written responses.

quickReference.domainLabel: Human Developmental and Individualized Learning Needs
quickReference.title: Complex Profiles, Communication Matrix, CVI & Medical Safety
quickReference.purpose: Anchors presymbolic-to-symbolic communication stages, CVI and deafblindness accommodations, motor/positioning safety, and school-health IHP/EAP protocols.
checklist: Assume communicative intent (presume competence) and map the student’s current communicative level from pre-intentional states through concrete and abstract symbols.
Verify visual (including Cortical Visual Impairment), hearing, tactile, respiratory, seizure, and orthopedic positioning requirements before starting any lesson.
Check the current nurse-authored Individualized Healthcare Plan (IHP) and Emergency Action Plan (EAP) before feeding, lifting, suctioning, or transporting a medically fragile student.
formulas: Rowland Communication Matrix 7 levels: (1) Pre-intentional behavior, (2) Intentional behavior, (3) Unconventional communication (pre-symbolic body/vocal acts), (4) Conventional communication (pointing, waving, head nods), (5) Concrete symbols (objects, photos, tangible symbols), (6) Abstract symbols (speech, manual signs, Braille, printed/AAC symbols), and (7) Language (combining 2+ symbols across four functions: Refuse, Obtain, Social, Information).

Cortical Visual Impairment (CVI, Roman-Lantzy) access rules: neurological visual-processing impairment (not ocular eye damage); support with color preference (often saturated red/yellow), movement cues, extended visual latency wait time, uncluttered solid-black backgrounds, reduced crowding/complexity, backlit targets, and preferred visual field positioning.

Deafblindness and tactile access: dual sensory loss creates unique communication and mobility barriers; use certified interveners, tactile/object calendars, hand-under-hand exploration (NEVER forceful hand-over-hand), and consistent personal-identifier touch cues before initiating interaction.

Medical fragility and physical positioning (IHP/EAP & Cedar Rapids v. Garret F.): IDEA requires continuous non-physician school-health services (tracheostomy suctioning, G-tube feeding, catheterization, seizure rescue meds/VNS magnet) needed for school attendance; follow PT/OT positioning schedules (reposition regularly to prevent pressure sores/contractures) and two-person/mechanical lift safety protocols.
decisionRules: When a student with CVI looks away whenever presented with a busy 12-symbol communication board under bright glare → prioritize simplifying visual complexity onto a matte black backlit display with 2 to 4 high-contrast saturated symbols and generous visual wait time.

When a student with deafblindness pulls their hand back during tactile exploration of a science model → prioritize shifting to hand-under-hand guidance with an advance touch-identifier cue so the student controls tactile contact.

When a nonspeaking student with severe multiple disabilities consistently looks toward a preferred music switch and vocalizes → prioritize treating the behavior as intentional communication, pairing a concrete symbol or single-message voice-output switch, and responding contingently.

When a medically fragile student experiences an atypical seizure lasting longer than the threshold written in the EAP → prioritize executing the nurse-authored Emergency Action Plan immediately (protect airway/head, time the event, summon nurse/EMS per protocol) without placing objects in the mouth.
cautions: Never use forceful hand-over-hand manipulation with students who are deafblind or tactilely defensive; hand-under-hand preserves autonomy and active exploration.
Do not confuse Cortical Visual Impairment with cognitive inability or inattention when visual clutter or short wait times prevent visual recognition.
Avoid performing invasive health procedures (G-tube feeding, tracheostomy suctioning, rectal/nasal rescue medications) without documented nurse training, delegation, and an active IHP/EAP.

quickReference.domainLabel: Planning and Instruction and the Learning Environment
quickReference.title: Partial Participation, Systematic Prompts, Inclusion & PBS
quickReference.purpose: Anchors the Principle of Partial Participation, embedded inclusive instruction, errorless systematic prompting, and medically screened Positive Behavior Support.
checklist: Apply the Principle of Partial Participation to identify meaningful, chronological-age-appropriate steps a student can perform with adaptations inside general-education and community routines.
Check for undiagnosed pain, GI reflux, ear infections, constipation, sleep loss, or communication breakdown first whenever severe self-injury or agitation escalates.
Select an explicit prompt-transfer system (Constant Time Delay, Simultaneous Prompting, System of Least Prompts, or Most-to-Least) with written fading criteria.
formulas: Principle of Partial Participation (Baumgart et al.): all students with severe disabilities can participate meaningfully in chronological-age-appropriate inclusive classrooms and community activities when teams adapt materials, sequences, rules, assistive technology (switches/AAC), or personal assistance—never require "prerequisite readiness" before inclusion.

Embedded instruction and Grade-Aligned Access: map IEP goals onto an instructional matrix across general-education schedules; pair peer-mediated supports and adapted grade-level texts (read-alouds, response boards, core vocabulary) with high-priority functional routines.

Systematic errorless and response-prompting methods: Simultaneous Prompting (daily probe trial before 0-second prompt instructional trials), Constant Time Delay (0s then 4 to 5s), Most-to-Least (MTL—preferred for motor/safety/error-sensitive tasks), System of Least Prompts (SLP), and total-task/backward chaining.

Intensive PBS and FCT for severe challenging behavior: conduct medical rule-out + comprehensive FBA (escape, attention, tangible, automatic/sensory/pain), pair Functional Communication Training (FCT via AAC/switch/tangible symbol) with Noncontingent Reinforcement (NCR) and antecedent enrichment; restrict emergency crisis interventions solely to imminent serious physical harm.
decisionRules: When a team argues a 10th grader with profound multiple disabilities cannot join biology lab because they cannot read the lab manual → prioritize applying Partial Participation by assigning an adapted switch-activated timer, tactile specimen sorting, and peer-partnered data recording.

When a nonspeaking student with severe disabilities suddenly begins head-banging after months of calm participation → prioritize immediate medical/pain/sensory screening alongside FBA before assuming attention-seeking behavior.

When teaching a student with severe motor and cognitive disabilities to activate a single-switch voice-output communicator for a turn → prioritize Simultaneous Prompting or 0s-to-5s Constant Time Delay with optimal switch positioning verified by the OT/PT.

When a student with complex communication needs screams to escape noisy group transitions → prioritize teaching an accessible AAC/card break request (FCT), adding noise-dampening headphones and visual/tactile transition warnings, and reinforcing calm requests immediately.
cautions: Never require a student with severe disabilities to "earn" general-education inclusion by first mastering isolated readiness skills in a segregated room.
Do not confuse sensory stereotypy or pain-driven distress with willful aggression, and never apply aversive punishers or routine seclusion/restraint.
Avoid letting paraprofessionals complete steps FOR the student out of haste; provide just-enough assistive prompting and full processing wait time.

quickReference.title: Accessible Assessment, Alternate Response Modes & Functional Data
quickReference.purpose: Anchors non-biased accessible assessment, floor-effect safeguards, ESSA 1% AA-AAS participation rules, and prompt-level visual progress analysis.
checklist: Confirm that the student’s established communication system, eye-gaze array, switch access, or partner-assisted scanning is embedded throughout every assessment task.
Avoid interpreting standardized test floor effects or motor-speech barriers as absence of learning or cognitive capacity.
Track trial-by-trial independence and prompt hierarchy levels frequently enough to revise stalled instruction within 1 to 2 weeks.
formulas: Accessible response modes and dynamic assessment: adapt assessment input/output via eye gaze, partner-assisted auditory/visual scanning, single/dual switches, tangible object symbols, and reduced-field choices; pair ecological inventories, caregiver interviews, and portfolio/dynamic test-teach-retest assessment to capture true learning potential.

Psychometric cautions for severe/profound profiles: norm-referenced IQ tests often suffer severe floor effects and violate standardization when sensory/motor/AAC access is required; report qualitative functional strengths, support needs, and validated alternate/criterion-referenced evidence alongside careful disclaimers.

ESSA 1% AA-AAS accountability framework (34 CFR 200.6(c)): Alternate Assessments aligned to Alternate Academic Achievement Standards measure grade-level academic content at reduced depth/breadth/complexity for students with the most significant cognitive disabilities; requires IEP team decision against state criteria, annual parent diploma-impact notice, and ongoing grade-aligned instruction.

Continuous functional data analysis: record task-analysis percent steps independent, prompt-level codes (I, V, G, M, PP, FP), response latency, and duration/frequency of communicative acts; apply data-decision rules (flat or descending trend across 3 to 5 consecutive sessions triggers prompt, antecedent, reinforcer, or access modification).
decisionRules: When a standardized achievement subtest requires timed pencil marking from a student with spastic quadriplegia → prioritize substituting accessible partner-assisted scanning, eye gaze, or dynamic ecological assessment rather than recording zero scores that reflect motor barriers.

When an IEP team determines a student with profound intellectual and multiple disabilities meets state criteria for AA-AAS → prioritize documenting the rationale in the IEP, notifying parents regarding diploma implications, and aligning daily instruction to state Alternate Achievement Standards.

When trial-by-trial data show a student stays at 30% independent steps for four consecutive sessions with errors clustering on grasping the switch → prioritize consulting the OT/AT specialist to adjust switch angle/sensitivity before concluding the student cannot learn the skill.

When preparing a triennial reevaluation for a student whose medical and communication needs remain stable → prioritize reviewing existing functional/progress data with parents (34 CFR 300.305) to identify only the targeted new assessments genuinely needed for instructional and transition planning.
cautions: Never report an "untestable" label that terminates evaluation; IDEA requires gathering functional, ecological, observational, and accessible assessment evidence to plan FAPE.
Do not administer an assessment using an unfamiliar switch or eye-gaze layout that the student has not practiced during routine instruction.
Avoid collecting anecdotal notes once per quarter instead of structured weekly prompt-level data on core IEP objectives.

quickReference.domainLabel: Ethical and Legal Practice, Professionalism, and Collaboration
quickReference.title: Transdisciplinary Teaming, Related Services, Privacy & Advocacy
quickReference.purpose: Anchors IDEA related-service mandates, transdisciplinary role release, paraprofessional training/supervision, personal-care dignity, and adult-transition legal rights.
checklist: Confirm that related services (PT, OT, SLP, orientation and mobility, vision/hearing specialists, school nursing) are embedded into natural daily routines rather than fragmented silos.
Maintain strict bodily privacy, universal health precautions, two-person lift safety, and dignity-centered language during all personal-care routines.
Verify that paraprofessionals follow teacher-designed instructional and safety plans while teachers lead evaluation, IEP design, and family conferences.
formulas: IDEA Related Services and LRE presumption (34 CFR 300.34 & 300.114): districts must provide transportation and developmental, corrective, and supportive services (SLP, OT, PT, audiology, school health/nursing, O&M, assistive technology) required to benefit from special education; severity of disability NEVER nullifies LRE consideration or FAPE entitlement (Timothy W. v. Rochester, zero-reject principle).

Transdisciplinary role release and integrated therapy: PT, OT, SLP, TVI, and school nurse train classroom staff to embed positioning, AAC, CVI, and motor targets across the entire school day while retaining specialist oversight for safety-critical clinical assessments and adjustments.

Personal-care dignity, safety, and mandated reporting: adhere to OSHA bloodborne-pathogen universal precautions, mechanical/two-person transfer rules, closed-door privacy during feeding/toileting/catheterization, and immediate mandated reporting for any suspected abuse or neglect of vulnerable students.

Adult transition and rights transfer (age 16 to 21): link families early with state developmental disability services, Medicaid waivers, Vocational Rehabilitation, community residential/day supports, and Supported Decision-Making (or limited guardianship options if necessary) at least 1 year before age of majority, plus a comprehensive Summary of Performance at exit.
decisionRules: When a district official claims a student with profound multiple disabilities is "too medically complex to benefit from education" → prioritize invoking IDEA’s zero-reject FAPE mandate (Timothy W. v. Rochester) and school-nursing entitlement (Cedar Rapids v. Garret F.) to ensure full educational access.

When an OT recommends hand-splint wearing times and adaptive utensil grips that never happen during cafeteria lunch → prioritize scheduling transdisciplinary role-release coaching so classroom staff and paraprofessionals integrate OT protocols seamlessly during real meals.

When a paraprofessional transfers a 110-pound student alone to save time despite a two-person/Hoyer-lift requirement → prioritize halting unsafe solo lifting immediately, retraining on the PT/nursing transfer protocol, and ensuring proper staffing coverage.

When a 19-year-old with profound disabilities approaches age-21 exit from public schooling → prioritize multi-agency transition meetings with adult developmental-disability coordinators, medical-transition teams, and family advocates to prevent a post-graduation services cliff.
cautions: Never perform personal-care or medical routines in open classroom view or discuss intimate health details casually in front of peers or visitors.
Do not allow related-service therapists to operate in disconnected pull-out silos without sharing AAC vocabulary, positioning schedules, and communication goals with classroom staff and families.
Avoid delaying adult-agency referrals until age 20, as Medicaid waiver and adult developmental-disability support waitlists often span multiple years.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Violating Presumed Competence or Requiring Cognitive Prerequisites Before AAC
misconceptionFamilies.description: Withholding Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) until a student proves object permanence, cause-and-effect mastery, or picture-matching skills (the debunked candidacy/prerequisite model), or dismissing presymbolic cues such as eye gaze, vocalizations, and muscle-tone shifts as non-communicative.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Operate from the Principle of Presumed Competence and the Communication Bill of Rights: apply zero cognitive prerequisites for AAC access, treat every presymbolic movement, gaze shift, or vocalization as potentially communicative, and immediately shape intentionality through responsive partner interaction.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Limiting AAC to Snack Requesting Instead of Core Vocabulary and Aided Language Modeling
misconceptionFamilies.description: Restricting a student's AAC system to fringe nouns for food requesting ("more," "cracker"), relying on intrusive hand-over-hand forcing to press icons, or leaving the device locked on a shelf during academic and social routines instead of modeling robust core vocabulary via Aided Language Stimulation.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Ensure 24/7 accessible AAC across all settings using high-frequency core vocabulary (go, stop, want, not, like, help, different) paired with relevant fringe words, model language naturally on the student's system (Aided Language Input) across varied functions (protesting, commenting, greeting, questioning), and use respectful hand-under-hand or expectant waiting rather than hand-over-hand compliance.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Equating Inclusion with Full Independent Mastery Instead of the Principle of Partial Participation
misconceptionFamilies.description: Excluding students with severe, profound, or multiple disabilities from general education classes, labs, or community routines because they cannot execute every step independently, rather than designing meaningful roles via the Principle of Partial Participation, switch/AT access, peer supports, and embedded IEP goals.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Apply the Principle of Partial Participation: analyze the natural general education or community routine, identify which steps the student can perform directly or with assistive technology/adaptations, embed individualized IEP goals inside shared activities, and coach peers as collaborative partners rather than passive helpers.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Performing Unauthorized Medical Procedures Outside an IHP or Neglecting Positioning and Seizure Safety
misconceptionFamilies.description: Allowing teachers or paraprofessionals to perform specialized health procedures (tracheostomy suctioning, G-tube bolus feeding, emergency seizure medication) without a school-nurse-developed Individualized Healthcare Plan (IHP), legal delegation, and verified competency training—or overlooking OT/PT positioning schedules, skin-integrity checks, and safe mechanical/two-person transfers.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Follow strict medical-delegation and safety boundaries: require a current written IHP and Emergency Action Plan authored by the licensed school nurse with documented delegation and competency verification before any staff member performs healthcare tasks, rotate positioning per OT/PT schedules to prevent pressure sores/contractures, and follow exact seizure-safety and safe-lifting protocols.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Using Floor-Effect Standardized Scores Instead of Ecological Inventory and Dynamic Assessment
misconceptionFamilies.description: Declaring a student with severe or multiple disabilities "untestable" because standardized norm-referenced IQ or achievement tests produce basal floor effects, instead of conducting ecological inventories, discrepancy analyses, systematic preference assessments, Communication Matrix profiles, and sensory-channel evaluations (including Cortical Visual Impairment and tactile access).
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Replace invalid norm-referenced floor scores with ecological assessment (inventorying current/future environments and discrepancy-analyzing needed adaptations), systematic stimulus preference assessments, Communication Matrix mapping, and functional vision/hearing/motor access evaluations to build actionable IEP targets.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Defaulting to Full Guardianship Instead of Supported Decision-Making and Person-Centered Transition
misconceptionFamilies.description: Advising families that plenary (full) guardianship is automatically required when a student with severe disabilities turns 18 rather than presenting least-restrictive alternatives such as Supported Decision-Making (SDM), or planning adult life around segregated facility slots without person-centered planning (MAPS/PATH) and early adult-services linkages.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Inform students and families at least one year before the age of majority about transfer of IDEA rights and the full continuum of decision-making supports (Supported Decision-Making agreements, power of attorney, healthcare proxy, representative payee, limited guardianship before plenary guardianship), and anchor adult transition in person-centered planning plus early Medicaid waiver, developmental disability agency, and customized-employment referrals.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Violating Presumed Competence or Requiring Cognitive Prerequisites Before AAC
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Honor Presumed Competence and Reject AAC Cognitive Prerequisites
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A 5547 team member argues that a student with profound multiple disabilities is "not ready" for an eye-gaze SGD or tactile symbols until they pass a cause-and-effect switch test, or ignores subtle body-state cues as random reflexes.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Are we presuming competence with zero cognitive prerequisites for AAC access, and responding consistently to presymbolic cues so the learner discovers communicative power?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Spot candidacy-model gatekeeping (demanding object permanence, picture discrimination, or verbal imitation before introducing AAC) and identify presymbolic communicative behaviors in the vignette (eye gaze, head turn, facial brightening, breath change, vocalization).
stages.requiredOutput: Flag the debunked prerequisite barrier in the distractor and list the student's observable presymbolic communicative signals.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Apply the National Joint Committee (NJC) Communication Bill of Rights and the progression from pre-intentional behavior → intentional presymbolic communication → concrete/tactile symbols → abstract symbols/speech-generating devices, explaining how consistent partner responsiveness builds intentionality rather than waiting for readiness.
stages.requiredOutput: Write a two-part clinical principle explaining why zero-exclusion AAC access accelerates—never inhibits—natural speech and cognitive engagement.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: A 7-year-old with cerebral palsy and Cortical Visual Impairment (CVI) widens her eyes and kicks her right foot when music stops, yet staff say she is too low-functioning for an AAC evaluation. Design the immediate team response.
stages.requiredOutput: Initiate an interdisciplinary AAC/AT evaluation (SLP, OT, TVI) matching access to her reliable motor/visual channels (such as high-contrast tactile symbols or single-message switch with CVI lighting accommodations) and create a Personal Communication Dictionary for all partners.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Evaluate a fresh 5547 item where a parent worries that introducing a tablet speech-generating device will stop their non-speaking child from ever learning to talk.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the research-grounded response reassuring the parent that AAC supports and often enhances natural vocalization while providing immediate dignity and communication access.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Limiting AAC to Snack Requesting Instead of Core Vocabulary and Aided Language Modeling
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Build Robust Core-Vocabulary AAC Through Aided Language Stimulation Across Functions
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A student's communication board contains only six snack icons, staff physically push the student's finger onto buttons hand-over-hand, or the SGD stays packed in a backpack during inclusive science and lunch.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does the student have continuous access to flexible core vocabulary across multiple communicative functions—and are communication partners modeling on the system naturally without intrusive hand-over-hand forcing?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Audit the AAC implementation in the vignette for four common breakdowns: snack-request-only fringe boards, hand-over-hand physical compliance, device unavailability across settings, and expecting the student to use a symbol system no adult ever models.
stages.requiredOutput: Identify the exact AAC implementation error in the stem and state which communicative functions (commenting, protesting, requesting help, asking questions, social greeting) are missing.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Contrast Core Vocabulary (roughly 80% of daily speech—flexible pronouns, verbs, descriptors like "more," "stop," "go," "not," "help," "turn," usable in every room) with Fringe Vocabulary (activity-specific nouns), and apply Aided Language Input/Stimulation (partners point to symbols while speaking naturally, wait expectantly 10+ seconds, honor every spontaneous attempt, and use respectful hand-under-hand guidance only when invited by learners with visual/motor needs).
stages.requiredOutput: Map four high-utility core words across three different school contexts (art, science, recess) and explain why modeling without demanding immediate repetition builds authentic AAC fluency.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: A tenth grader uses a high-tech eye-gaze SGD only to request juice during break time; during English class his device is turned off because "it distracts the class." Redesign his daily AAC plan.
stages.requiredOutput: Require continuous mounted SGD access throughout English, add literature core/fringe phrases ("I think," "disagree," "read more," character names), train teachers and peers in Aided Language Modeling, and give a 10-second response pause.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Solve a new 5547 item asking why teaching a student to activate "stop" or "all done" on an AAC device is an essential first target alongside requesting preferred items.
stages.requiredOutput: Select honoring the right to refuse/protest safely, which empowers self-advocacy and replaces frustration-driven challenging behavior.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Equating Inclusion with Full Independent Mastery Instead of the Principle of Partial Participation
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Operationalize Partial Participation, Adapted Access, and Embedded IEP Goals
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A vignette excludes a student with severe disabilities from a general education biology lab, choir, or school store because they cannot read the lab manual or manipulate fine glassware independently.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Which meaningful steps of this shared activity can the student execute directly or through switch/AT adaptations and peer collaboration under the Principle of Partial Participation?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Spot the "all-or-nothing mastery" fallacy—assuming that inability to complete 100% of a task independently justifies segregating the student into an isolated classroom or having an aide sit passively beside them doing the task for them.
stages.requiredOutput: Flag the all-or-nothing exclusion or adult-velcro trap in the distractor and locate the shared classroom routine.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Run the four-step Partial Participation design process: (1) list the natural sequence peers follow in the general education or community routine, (2) identify steps the student performs independently, (3) engineer individualized adaptations for remaining steps (switch-activated blender/timer, adapted grip, partner-assisted scanning, simplified visual steps, natural peer collaboration), and (4) embed measurable IEP communication, motor, and grade-aligned academic goals directly into those moments.
stages.requiredOutput: Explain how Partial Participation differs from passive physical presence (sitting in the back watching) and how natural peer supports reduce adult-aide stigma.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Design a Partial Participation plan for a sixth grader with profound intellectual and motor disabilities joining an inclusive science lab on plant growth where peers measure soil, water seedlings, and log observations.
stages.requiredOutput: Assign authentic active roles: activating a switch-adapted battery water pump to water the group's plant, choosing the observation picture/core-word label ("tall," "wet") via eye gaze or big-mac switch to report group findings, and sharing lab turns with trained peers.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-read a 5547 inclusion item asking how to embed a student's IEP goal for activating a choice switch inside a general education music class.
stages.requiredOutput: Choose an authentic musical role (using a switch-adapted instrument or selecting the next class song on a step-by-step communicator during chorus transitions) rather than pulling the student into the hallway to drill switch hits.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Performing Unauthorized Medical Procedures Outside an IHP or Neglecting Positioning and Seizure Safety
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Follow Nurse-Directed IHP Delegation, Safe Transfers, Positioning, and Seizure Protocols
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A teacher or paraprofessional is asked to administer rectal or intranasal rescue seizure medication, suction a tracheostomy, or feed via G-tube based on an informal parent note—or leaves a non-ambulatory student in one wheelchair position all day.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Is this medical or physical care task authorized inside a current nurse-authored IHP with verified state-legal delegation and competency training, and are positioning, skin-integrity, and seizure-safety protocols strictly followed?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Scan the vignette for healthcare scope-of-practice violations (untrained staff performing invasive procedures, acting on verbal parent requests without physician orders/nurse IHP), unsafe one-person lifts, or dangerous seizure myths (putting objects in the mouth, restraining convulsing limbs).
stages.requiredOutput: Identify the exact medical-delegation, positioning, or emergency-safety hazard in the distractor.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Anchor four non-negotiable health and physical safety standards: (1) Medical Delegation (requires physician orders, school-nurse-authored IHP and Emergency Care Plan, compliance with the state Nurse Practice Act, documented hands-on competency sign-off, and ongoing RN supervision), (2) Positioning & Mobility (follow OT/PT positioning schedules across wheelchair, stander, and side-lyer to protect respiration, digestion, and skin integrity; inspect for redness; use two-person or mechanical Hoyer lifts), (3) Feeding/Swallowing Safety (strict dysphagia diet textures, upright alignment, aspiration red-flag alerts), and (4) Seizure First Aid (ease safely to floor, turn on side, cushion head, time duration, never place anything in mouth or restrain, follow IHP rescue-med/911 triggers).
stages.requiredOutput: State the three prerequisites before a teacher can legally perform a delegated medical procedure and list the four immediate safety steps during a tonic-clonic seizure.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: A parent hands a special education teacher a new bottle of liquid seizure medication at morning drop-off and asks the teacher to give it if the student stares blankly for two minutes. Specify the legally and medically safe response.
stages.requiredOutput: Route the medication immediately to the school nurse, verify written physician orders and signed parent authorization, update the student's IHP/Seizure Action Plan, and complete formal nurse-delegated training before any classroom administration.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Evaluate a fresh 5547 physical-care vignette where a paraprofessional notices persistent redness over a non-ambulatory student's hip after a long wheelchair block.
stages.requiredOutput: Select immediate repositioning per OT/PT plan, alerting the school nurse and family to prevent pressure ulcer breakdown, and reviewing seating cushion alignment with OT/PT.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Using Floor-Effect Standardized Scores Instead of Ecological Inventory and Dynamic Assessment
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Conduct Ecological Inventories, Preference Assessments, and Sensory-Channel Evaluations
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: An assessment item shows a student with profound multiple disabilities scoring at the absolute floor of a norm-referenced IQ battery ("untestable"), and asks how the team should gather valid PLAAFP data to drive meaningful IEP goals.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: How do we gather ecologically valid functional data—through ecological inventories, discrepancy analysis, systematic preference assessment, Communication Matrix mapping, and functional sensory evaluations—instead of stopping at floor-effect test scores?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Identify why standardized norm-referenced instruments break down for students with severe/profound or sensory-motor disabilities (floor effects, motor/verbal response bias, lack of instructional utility) and spot distractors that label a student "untestable."
stages.requiredOutput: Explain the validity failure of the norm-referenced distractor and name the functional assessment domain needed (environment, preference, communication, or sensory channel).

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Match four high-yield severe-disabilities assessment tools to their exact instructional output: (1) Ecological Inventory & Discrepancy Analysis (catalogs current/future environments → sub-environments → activities → natural peer steps → student discrepancy → instruction or adaptation plan), (2) Systematic Preference Assessment (single-stimulus, paired-choice, or MSWO to empirically identify potent reinforcers), (3) Communication Matrix (maps expressive modes across 7 levels from pre-intentional to language), and (4) Functional Vision/Learning Media & Audiological Assessment (distinguishes ocular vs. Cortical Visual Impairment, optimal visual field, lighting, and tactile/auditory access).
stages.requiredOutput: Pair each of the four tools with one concrete IEP decision it informs.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: A newly enrolled 9-year-old with deaf-blindness and severe motor impairment arrives with a report reading "unable to establish basal; cognitive functioning untestable." Design a four-part comprehensive evaluation plan.
stages.requiredOutput: Combine a Functional Vision/Hearing and Learning Media Assessment (TVI/TOD), a tactile/micro-switch preference assessment, a Communication Matrix with family input, and an Ecological Inventory of classroom, cafeteria, and mobility routines.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Solve a new 5547 assessment vignette asking how to determine whether a student with profound disabilities who does not reach for toys prefers vibration, music, or warm light as a reinforcer.
stages.requiredOutput: Select a systematic single-stimulus (or paired-choice) preference assessment tracking observable approach/affective indicators (smiling, orienting, sustained vocalization, reduced withdrawal) across repeated trials.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Defaulting to Full Guardianship Instead of Supported Decision-Making and Person-Centered Transition
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Center Dignity of Risk, Supported Decision-Making, and Interagency Adult Transition
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A secondary transition team tells parents they must file for full legal guardianship before their 17-year-old with severe disabilities turns 18, or defaults the student to a segregated day program without person-centered planning or early Medicaid/adult-agency links.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Have we informed the student and family about Supported Decision-Making and least-restrictive legal options before guardianship, while using person-centered planning and early adult-agency linkages to build a self-determined adult life?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Spot paternalistic transition traps: treating plenary guardianship as mandatory at age 18, excluding a non-speaking student from their own transition meeting, or waiting until graduation month to contact adult developmental-disability agencies (which often have multi-year waitlists).
stages.requiredOutput: Identify the autonomy, transfer-of-rights, or interagency-timing breakdown in the distractor.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Sequence the least-restrictive adult-transition safeguards: (1) notify student and parents at least one year before age of majority regarding IDEA transfer of rights, (2) present the decision-making continuum from least to most restrictive (Supported Decision-Making agreements → educational/healthcare proxy or power of attorney → representative payee → limited guardianship → plenary guardianship only as last resort), (3) use Person-Centered Planning (MAPS, PATH, Essential Lifestyle Planning) incorporating the student's AAC/communication preferences, and (4) initiate interagency linkages early (with written consent) for Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) waivers, state DD agencies, Vocational Rehabilitation/customized employment, and SSI/ABLE financial planning.
stages.requiredOutput: Order four decision-making options from least to most restrictive and explain why Medicaid HCBS waiver and DD-agency referrals must start years before age 21/22 exit.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Parents of a 17-year-old with profound ID and complex medical needs tell the IEP team they heard they must obtain full guardianship to stay involved in IEP meetings and doctor visits after age 18. Draft the team's accurate, respectful guidance.
stages.requiredOutput: Clarify that IDEA requires transfer-of-rights notice (never mandating guardianship), outline least-restrictive options such as Supported Decision-Making and healthcare/educational power of attorney alongside legal-aid consultation, and invite the student via AAC/visual preference boards to co-lead a PATH person-centered plan.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-read a 5547 transition vignette asking how a transition coordinator should pursue employment for a 20-year-old with multiple disabilities who uses a wheelchair and eye-gaze AAC.
stages.requiredOutput: Select Discovery and Customized Employment carved around the student's strengths, assistive technology, and natural workplace supports in competitive integrated settings rather than defaulting to sheltered workshops.
